newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Anti-Taleban forces make gains in Afghan northwest.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban forces make gains in Afghan northwest.

text.p: The forces of a northern alliance have pushed back the purist Islamic Taleban militia in fighting in the remote northwest of Afghanistan, reliable sources said on Tuesday.

The Taleban, who took Kabul a month ago, have said their forces captured Badghis province on the border with Turkmenistan late last week and were driving on to Maimana, capital of neighbouring Faryab.
But the sources said 2,000 men sent by northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum to meet the threat on a new front in Afghanistan's latest war had counter-attacked successfully.
There was also fighting north of Kabul on Tuesday between the Taleban and forces of the northern alliance, witnesses said.

The Kabul-based sources, who have contacts with northwest Afghanistan, said Dostum forces led by General Malik, who uses only one name, captured the town of Bala Morghab, some 60 km (38 miles) inside Badghis province on Sunday.
"Yesterday, there was fighting near Qalaye-i-Naw," said one source of the Badghis capital another 80 km (50 miles) into the province. "Our information is that General Malik is still advancing."

If Dostum could recapture Badghis, he would be in a position to threaten the western city of Herat where there is a substantial population of ethnic Tajiks, cousins to the people of Dostum ally Ahmad Shah Masood.
It could also open up the southern plains and allow the northern alliance to threaten Kandahar, the southern city where the Taleban have their headquarters.
Such a threat might force the Taleban to weaken their defences north of Kabul, where the front line has been static for a week.
"The Taleban are obviously strong enough to hold the front, but do not appear to be in a position to push Dostum and Masood back," said one Afghan watcher in Kabul.
"But if they are seriously threatened on a new front, and with so many Kandaharis fighting north of Kabul, they might not be able to sustain their defence of the city," he said.
Masood, the former government military chief, and Dostum have made repeated attempts to overcome Taleban defensive lines in hills snaking across the plain 25-30 km (15-19 miles) north of the capital.
Taleban fighters at the front line said the combined forces of the northern alliance tried again on Monday night but were repulsed.
There was no immediate confirmation of the report, but witnesses said the front lines had not changed.
Reuters correspondent Chris Bird reported that a Taleban plane was in action on Tuesday, bombing Masood positions below the De Sabz pass 30 km (20 miles) north of the Afghan capital.
Five civilians were killed on Tuesday when a Taleban rocket hit their home in the nearby village of Kalakan.

The fighting on the front north of Kabul has involved some heavy fighting over the past week in which both sides have used warplanes to bomb each other's positions. The Taleban have also used helicopter gunships.
Dostum also tried three times over the weekend to bomb Kabul airport, which is used for both civilian and military traffic.
Airport sources said the raids failed to damage the airport, which is on the northeast fringe of the city.
Thousands of people have fled villages in the combat zone, some heading to Kabul and others to the north and west, aid workers say.
There has been no reliable account of civilian casualties, but the aid workers said they appeared to have been heavy.
